title: TRAI's draft AI rules would make telecom operators answerable for vendors' AI and report serious failures
dek: The regulator's consultation paper proposes board-approved AI policies, risk classes and mandatory reporting of the most serious AI incidents.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) has released draft guidelines on the responsible use of artificial intelligence in telecom, proposing that licensed operators be held accountable for the outcomes of every AI system they use, including systems bought from outside vendors. The draft is a consultation paper, not a final rule, and the regulator is seeking public comments, according to reports by Business Standard, MediaNama and Indian Television.

## What the draft proposes

The draft applies to licensed telecom service providers and network operators that use, or plan to use, AI in their networks or services. As reported, its main proposals are:

- Board-approved AI policies at each operator, with risk classification of AI systems and human oversight.
- Accountability for third-party AI: operators buying equipment, software or services with AI built in would have to obtain disclosures from suppliers, and supplier contracts would need audit rights and incident-management terms.
- Incident reporting: AI incidents would be sorted into four severity levels, with mandatory reporting to the regulator for the top two, critical and high.
- Records: a central database of AI incidents, plus a separate record of AI harm reported by consumers.

## What is not yet settled

Reports say the draft does not define what counts as a critical or high-severity incident, and does not fix the time within which mandatory reporting must happen. It also does not create a separate penalty framework. One report puts the last date for comments at November 27; we have not been able to check that against the paper itself, so readers should treat the date as unconfirmed.

## Why it matters

Telecom operators already use machine-learning tools for network planning, fraud detection and customer service, and increasingly buy them as part of vendor packages. Making the operator, rather than the vendor, answerable for outcomes would shift due diligence to the companies that hold the licence and the customer relationship. The draft arrives alongside other official moves on digital security: MeitY Secretary S Krishnan said on 24 October that CERT-In had flagged about 60,000 Indian websites as potentially vulnerable, a figure we could not confirm in a CERT-In notice, and a report by Elets eGov says the Centre is weighing giving CERT-In binding powers to force government bodies to patch critical flaws.

## What happens next

TRAI will take comments, may hold open discussions and then issue final recommendations or directions. Operators and industry bodies are expected to argue over the definitions of severity levels and the reach of vendor accountability. A separate MeitY consultation on AI regulation was reported as expected in early November, but we have not seen it released.

We did not find the paper on TRAI's own website at the time of writing, so this report is based on outlet coverage of the draft. We will update when the document can be read directly.
